content.thinking:
I'm planning the elephant's skeleton structure, starting with the pelvis joint and spine chain positions to build a realistic proportioned body facing forward.

I'm then mapping out the neck leading to a sizeable head, and designing the trunk as a multi-joint curve dropping down and curling forward at the tip. For the legs, I'm placing front and hind limbs at appropriate x/z offsets with columnar lengths and bend directions suited to an elephant's forward-facing knee joints.

Writing leg sweep code...

Also need to add toenails and a foot cylinder bone, and watch out that a rounded end-cap on the leg sweep would push the radius below floor level at the foot—better use a flat cap there instead.

Now thinking about the body: I'll loft or sweep along the spine with a bone list, considering whether to build a separate spine chain from rump to chest versus reusing the leg chain's joints, and setting up the pelvis root position accordingly.

Adding the head joint off the neck's final point, then starting the tail chain from the rump, dropping down and back behind the pelvis.

I'm also figuring out how the body sweep path connects to the pelvis root joint and spine chain — since pelvis is the root with no aim constraint, it keeps a default orientation, and the first spine joint overlaps it at nearly the same position.

For bone ownership when joints share a parameter t, I'll let the later listed joint (spine1) take precedence over pelvis for that span, so the body loft runs along [spine, neck]. I'm sketching the body stations now — rump dimensions, barrel width/height around the spine joints — to approximate the elephant's torso shape.

Now I'm defining the head stations, placing them forward from the body end to form the skull shape with appropriate widths and heights tapering toward the trunk area.

Setting up the head joint and a small jaw joint beneath the trunk base, with a short box piece for the lower lip hidden under the trunk since elephants' jaws aren't very visible.

Now I'm thinking through the ears -- shaped roughly like Africa, attached near the side of the head and flaring outward and down, which I'll build as an extruded flap on a tilted plane near the head.

Working out the ear shape coordinates, tracing a polygon outline from the top-front attachment point back and down to form a flared, rounded ear silhouette.

Adding inner ear shading geometry...

Now moving on to the tusks: I'll sweep curved ivory shapes outward and upward from the head using bezier control points for a natural tusk curve.

I'll color the tusks with an ivory gradient from darker base to lighter tip, then build the trunk as a curved chain of points from the head down toward the floor, tapering radius from 0.3 at the base down to narrower near the curling tip, keeping it above ground level.

Adding ring ridge texture via a fractional striping pattern along the trunk's length, plus small finger-like cones near the tip for the nostril detail. For coloring, I'm setting a greyish-brown base palette with darker and lighter variants, and planning a dust-brown gradient on the lower legs.

Now I'm layering coat textures: a mottled grey-brown base paint, then overlaying wavy crease stripes with wobble and noise to simulate wrinkled skin across the body.

Then I'm applying countershading so the belly reads slightly lighter and pinkish-grey underneath, reusing the same wrinkled coat paint on the head for consistency, and planning the eyes as small dark spheres with an amber ring set into the side of the head.

For eye placement, I'm figuring out the proper surface point by interpolating the head loft's width between stations near the eye's z-position, then worrying that a fixed offset might float above or sink below the curved surface. I'll switch to casting a ray against the head surface to find the exact contact point and stick the eye there instead of guessing a radius.

Then I'm layering eye details: an amber iris ring embedded slightly into the socket, a darker pupil sphere on top, and considering whether to add lashes or a brow ridge before deciding to keep it simple with just an eyelid rim.

Next I'm sketching forehead dome bumps on the head using scaled spheres positioned near the top, cross-checking the head bone's height range against the body's top to figure out proper placement.

Now I'm turning to toe nails: placing small boxes around the front edge of each foot (five on front legs, four on rear) arranged in an angled arc, oriented outward from the toe tips.

I'm referencing the leg's tip joint for foot positioning, then considering adding knee bulge details—small sphere bumps at knee joints for front and hind legs to suggest wrinkles and joint structure.

Now I'm working out leg thickness profiles, varying radii along the sweep for front versus hind legs, and checking that leg root positions sit correctly within the body's width and height so the legs attach naturally under the torso without poking through the sides.

For the limb chains, I'm computing root-to-target distances and segment lengths for both front and hind legs to confirm the reach works with a slight knee bend, then settling on joint naming conventions like hip/knee/ankle so each chain gets the right number of named points including a tip joint at the end.

Now I'm working out the leg skin sweeps using the chain as the sweep source, making sure the tube radius covers the foot cylinder at the flat end, and figuring out chain parenting -- front legs attaching to the spine and hind legs to the pelvis. For the tail, I'm planning a tapering sweep radius from base to tip, plus a tuft of dark spikes arranged in a ring around the tail's end.

I'm defining the tail-tip spikes as a fan of eight dark spikes at the final tail joint, using the last joint in the tail chain as the bone reference since the chain only has three named segments. I decide to skip extra anatomical details like skin folds at the legs or belly, leaving those to paint handles instead of added geometry, since ring-loop sweeps there risk looking wrong.

Now I'm writing a paint function for ear veins, computing an angle from the surface coordinates to create radiating stripe patterns using sine waves, so the veins fan out from the ear base with slight distortion for a natural look.

I'll skip adding a rim darkness gradient for now since the outline distance isn't readily available, and I'm deciding ear ruffle detail at the lower edge is fine as-is. I still need to add ear joints to the skeleton for rigging purposes.

Adding ear hinge joints...

Adding lighter belly coloring based on angle ranges for a pinker trunk underside, then adding sparse dark bristle spikes scattered on the forehead and head top for hair detail.

Skipping whiskers and dust clumps, but adding tusk base details—a darker flesh-colored cap sphere at the gum line and banded ivory-to-cream coloring toward the tip for a polished look. I'm positioning the tusk sweep path so it emerges naturally from inside the head geometry near the jaw area.

Checking the head loft stations and widths to make sure the tusk start point at roughly (0.32, 1.95, 2.2) sits inside the head surface, then tracing curve points so it emerges forward and downward around z~2.4-2.7 before sweeping to a tip near (0.38, 1.5, 3.7).

Settling on an overall height around 3.15 units as close enough to a real elephant's shoulder proportions, and confirming foot cylinders sit flush at y=0 with slightly flared pad geometry for front and leg bottoms.

I'm adding shoulder and hip muscle bulges as scaled spheres positioned along the spine, painted using position-based coat coloring to blend with the body's stripe pattern.

Going for a low-poly aesthetic, I'm reducing sweep sides across parts (body 10, legs/trunk 8, tusk 6) and turning off smooth shading so the facets catch the painted creases and mottling for a faceted, stylized look.

For the skeleton, I'm figuring out bone ownership along the spine and neck: the spine chain covers the rump and body, with pelvis as root joint, while the neck chain (with increasing radii toward the head) picks up where the body loft leaves off to connect smoothly into the head.

I'm checking the head and neck sweep parameters so the geometry connects cleanly without gaps, confirming all surfaces share the same coat paint, and verifying raycasting works against the head's swept mesh. I'm also cleaning up unused TypeScript imports like frame, aim, offset, and mix to avoid strict lint errors.

Now I'm importing the needed paint helpers (countershade, gradient, mottle, paint, stripes), the catmull path function, the limb IK solver, and the rng math utility. I'm making sure the chain names arrays match the correct point/span counts for the neck, spine, and trunk segments, and setting the trunk joints to a "tentacle" role while the spine chain gets its own role.

I'm assigning roles to the other chains—neck, tail, legs—and setting up the pelvis as the root spine joint. For the head, I'm sculpting dome bumps on the sphere and casting rays to place the eyes, skipping any ray that misses the surface and orienting the eye cylinders along the hit normal with the head bone as the weight target. Now I'm starting to sweep a small dark line for the mouth shape.

Still working out limb geometry...

Still writing gradient paint...

Now checking the trunk path geometry: verifying the curve from the head down through the trunk segments stays above ground and curls naturally at the tip, adjusting the final point to around (0,0.5,3.5) so the rounded cap reaches y=.4, giving a trunk length near 2.1 units, consistent with a real elephant's trunk.

I'm tapering the trunk radii from base to tip, adding a small dorsal finger spike near the trunk's end for the characteristic fingertip shape, plus a smaller ventral nub, then moving on to scatter some hair geometry across the head's surface.

Now I'm drafting the elephant's body builder code, importing geometry helpers and setting up the pelvis joint and spine chain using catmull-rom curves to define the skeleton's path.

Writing more skeleton joints...

I'm adjusting the ear's attachment point inward so it embeds slightly into the head surface rather than floating outside it, and setting up outline points with a sharp tip corner for the ear shape definition.

Still writing ear geometry...

I'm checking that the ear polygon stays simple after smoothing with its sharp corner, and planning the inner ear as a nested, slightly offset shape with its own color for depth.

Now I'm working out positioning for shoulder and hip bulges using sphere geometry attached to spine and pelvis bones, scaled and flattened to shape the body silhouette, with eyes to be added after the head loft completes.

For the tusks, I'm sweeping a curve through control points with tapered radii and a pointed cap, attached to the head bone with a gum base sphere. For the tail, I'm chaining sweep segments with decreasing radii and a rounded end cap, positioning it to emerge from the rump area of the body where it fits within the body's height span.

I'm adding a spiky tuft at the tail tip with a ring of eight directional spikes radiating outward and downward, bound to the last tail bone. I'm skipping extra details like body hair, dust clumps, and mole patches since the mottled coloring already provides enough texture variation.

For the mouth, I'm building the lower jaw as a simple box frustum shape bound to the jaw bone using the coat color. For the trunk, I'm defining a wrinkle paint function that creates periodic crease lines along the trunk's length and blends in pink coloring within a certain band, falling back to the base coat color elsewhere.

Now I'm setting up the eye geometry as a small cylinder shape, then finalizing the function to return the assembled root node. I'm double-checking the type signatures for the stick and scatter helper functions to make sure hit parameters and normals are handled correctly, and confirming the trunk sweep can accept the wrinkle paint as its color source before writing out the final file.
